content: Recurrent apnea is a frequent condition in preterm infants, especially those born at very early gestational ages. These episodes involve a temporary cessation of effective breathing, which can result in reduced oxygen levels in the blood (hypoxemia) and a slowed heart rate (bradycardia). In severe cases, these events may necessitate resuscitation measures, such as the use of positive pressure ventilation or other medical interventions. Physical stimulation is commonly employed to reinitiate breathing during such episodes. It has been hypothesized that repetitive physical stimulation, such as the use of an oscillating mattress (a form of kinesthetic stimulation), might help prevent apnea and its associated complications. The objective of this review was to evaluate whether prophylactic kinesthetic stimulation could reduce the incidence of apnea and bradycardia, as well as the need for intermittent positive pressure ventilation (IPPV), in preterm infants who are at risk of developing apnea. To address this question, the researchers employed the standard search strategy of the Cochrane Neonatal Review Group. This included comprehensive searches of multiple databases, such as the Oxford Database of Perinatal Trials, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (up to Issue 4, 2009), MEDLINE (from 1966 to October 2009), EMBASE, and CINAHL (from 1982 to October 2009). Additional sources included prior reviews, cross-referenced studies, conference proceedings, expert consultations, and hand-searching of relevant journals, primarily in the English language. The review included all trials involving preterm infants at risk of clinical apnea, where participants were randomly or quasi-randomly assigned to receive either treatment with an oscillating mattress (or other forms of repetitive kinesthetic stimulation) or a control intervention. Data collection and analysis followed the standard methods of the Cochrane Collaboration and its Neonatal Review Group. Each author independently assessed the quality of the trials and extracted data, which were then synthesized using relative risk as the measure of effect. Three trials, involving a total of 154 preterm infants, met the inclusion criteria for this review. The findings revealed no evidence that prophylactic kinesthetic stimulation had any effect on short-term outcomes, such as the frequency of apnea or bradycardia, the occurrence of intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH), the need for IPPV, sleep-wake cycles, or neurological status at the time of discharge. Additionally, in one trial that assessed long-term outcomes, no impact was observed on growth and developmental milestones up to one year of age. Based on these findings, the authors concluded that the prophylactic use of kinesthetic stimulation cannot be recommended as an effective intervention to reduce apnea or bradycardia in preterm infants. Furthermore, they noted that there are currently no well-defined research questions regarding the use of prophylactic kinesthetic stimulation for the prevention of apnea in this population.
